title: 1Xtra launches first ever UK rap chart for 'fair playing field'
description: British rap artists will step into the spotlight later when BBC Radio 1Xtra launches the first ever dedicated rap chart based on UK listening figures.
body: British rap artists will step into the spotlight later when BBC Radio 1Xtra launches the first ever dedicated rap chart based on UK listening figures.DJ Kenny Allstar, who'll host the countdown on Friday nights, has one word: "Finally"."If we have our own fair playing field where we can all be celebrated... it then feels fair and it feels exciting," he tells BBC Newsbeat.Currently artists compete across genres for a spot in the Official Singles Chart, but Allstar says this is dominated by pop music, making it harder for other genres to be heard.Perhaps with the exception of heavyweights like Central Cee and Dave, who broke chart records with Sprinter back in 2023, "it's not easy for any artist to go against Sabrina Carpenter and Taylor Swift every week," he says.Compiled by the Official Charts Company, 20 rap singles from British artists will be ranked each week based on streams and sales in the UK. It follows the launch of other genre-specific charts including for R&B, 'homegrown' albums and British Asian music.Allstar hopes it'll give UK rap a boost as he acknowledges it has taken a bit of a beating recently with prominent artists like Skepta and Digga saying the quality of music coming from the scene has dipped."I want to find solutions," he says. "Future broadcasters and talent will benefit from this forever, I'm super gassed."Allstar has long been a champion of UK rap and currently presents the Rap Show on BBC Radio 1, which he describes as "the show I always wanted as a kid".This new role is "a pinch me moment," he says.The Official Charts Company previously listed the 40 top selling R&B and hip hop tracks on its website, but there had been nowhere for fans to listen to the chart."It was literally just a bunch of numbers and text, so it kind of existed but not in this capacity," Allstar says.Each week will likely see at least three or four new artists in the chart, giving emerging talent a chance to be heard by hundreds of thousands of listeners. "What we can finally have is UK rap having its dedicated space where artists can just be celebrated," he says.Eric Hunter, from the Official Charts Company, says the countdown will be "an amazing opportunity to shine a light on more artists, document the culture and give emerging talent a way to track their progress alongside their peers".The company says UK rap is "one of the country's most influential and fast-moving music scenes" and the chart will celebrate both established names and the next generation of rappers driving the scene.The debut show coincides with Skepta's long-awaited sixth studio album and Allstar says he expects to see the rapper feature in the chart."It's looking promising, but the only way you can find out is if you listen in," he says.The Official UK Rap Chart will broadcast on 1Xtra each Friday from 22:00-23:00 and will be available after on BBC Sounds.

schema.headline: 1Xtra launches first ever UK rap chart for 'fair playing field'

title: Israel president asks opposition leader Eisenkot to form government
description: Israel's president says he will task opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new coalition government.Isaac Herzog has been holding talks with
body: Israel's president says he will task opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new coalition government.Isaac Herzog has been holding talks with political parties after neither Eisenkot's bloc nor that of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secured a majority in Israel's parliament, known as the Knesset, following last week's election.Eisenkot will now have 28 days to try to form a new administration, with a potential 14-day extension."Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy," the former military chief wrote on X.No political party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, meaning all governments have been coalitions.Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, while Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc won 48.Two Arab-led alliances, the United Arab List and the Joint List, together won an unprecedented 19 seats following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.That positions them as potential kingmakers. However, all but one of the Jewish parties pledged before the polls not to work with them to form a government.Herzog said that, after consulting all parties during the week, he would give Eisenkot the first chance to form a government.A statement from the president's office said he had informed both Eisenkot and Netanyahu of the decision.Following consultations with delegations from the incoming Knesset members, Eisenkot received 67 recommendations for the premiership and Netanyahu 46, the statement said.The president has broad discretion to pick someone they believe has the best chance of building a coalition and does not have to choose the leader of the party with the most seats.The election results had implied three possible options for the formation of a government: a national unity administration involving both Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a right-wing coalition involving Netanyahu and defectors from Eisenkot's bloc, or an Eisenkot-led government supported by the Arab parties.Eisenkot and every member of his bloc bar one has previously refused to enter government with Arab parties, but there has been speculation that an agreement could be reached.He could also attempt to reach a deal with ultra-Orthodox parties, but that too would be difficult.There is precedent for a unity government. In 2020, following three deadlocked elections, Netanyahu and his centrist rival Benny Gantz agreed a power-sharing deal in which the leadership rotated between the two.During his consultations with the parties, Herzog had said that to prevent another round of elections and to build a stable government, he expected "factions and their representatives to understand that, in the current reality, not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled".In the period 2019 to 2022, one of the most politically fractured in Israeli politics, there were five separate elections as Netanyahu and his rivals struggled time and again to co-operate.

schema.headline: Israel president asks opposition leader Eisenkot to form government

title: Duo-euthanasia: When your parents choose to die
description: Bas had planned a scenic route to the hospice, taking in Friesland's meadows and canals."I still remember the whole trip," he says. His mum was in the
body: Bas had planned a scenic route to the hospice, taking in Friesland's meadows and canals."I still remember the whole trip," he says. His mum was in the back seat and his dad sat beside him. At first, they talked. Els seemed resolute about their decision to opt for euthanasia."My mum was convinced, certain about doing it," Bas says. "But my dad was a little bit emotional."Jan asked his son if they were doing the right thing. Bas was thrown - he thought it would be his mum who might have doubts."My mum had always really enjoyed life," he says. "I remember she told me, 'I'd love to be 80 or maybe even 90 years old.'"But his father had been talking about euthanasia for more than a decade because of all the years of pain.In the car, Bas reassured his dad. Once Jan calmed down, they drove without speaking, listened to music and watched the scenery go by.Bas found a parking space."My dad said goodbye to my car - he liked my car, and he said, 'Good job', and 'thank you'."And then we walked inside," Bas says. "Imagine doing that - being in their shoes, taking that trip and that walk. It's so unreal."For the next two hours, the couple's family and friends came and went. They reminisced, and listened to music. At one point, it crossed Bas' mind to call a halt to the proceedings."I had a feeling - 'OK, let's leave… Let's step into the car and drive away,'" he says. "But I didn't want to bring anything up that would make them feel uncertain - I had supported the whole [euthanasia] process."Better to keep everybody calm, and take the moment to say goodbye."Where to get help- The Samaritans, external- Befrienders Worldwide, external- NHS Help for suicidal thoughts, external- BBC Action LineJust before 10:30am, doctors arrived to inject Jan and Els with the lethal medication that would kill them. The couple lay on hospital beds side by side. And in those final moments, before they lost consciousness, Bas witnessed his parents' closeness."I've seen them maybe three or four times in all my life walking hand in hand," he says. "But now they were laying there, hand in hand. And that gave me a really good feeling - they're really doing this together."Bas describes that first half hour after his parents stopped breathing as "a factual thing" - they weren't alive anymore."Then you realise what the situation is - that's an unimaginable feeling."In the hospice, sorrow hit Bas. He began to experience a profound loneliness."Grieving is a very, very deep thing to go through," he says, "and I don't have brothers and sisters - I really felt alone."If we've been brought up by two parents, when the first dies, we can share our memories and sadness with the other as part of the process of bereavement. But Jan and Els were both gone."It was like my legs were cut off," remembers Bas.His grief was physical too - he felt sick for four or five weeks. His body hurt."I would not really recommend this to others, and that's maybe a hard conclusion," he says. "It was maybe for them [my parents] the best option, but having lost them both at the same moment was very, very impactful."Among people planning to apply for euthanasia in the Netherlands, especially those with dementia like Els, choosing the right moment to end your life may be complicated.9,958 people in the Netherlands chose death by euthanasia in 2024427 of those who chose death by euthanasia in 2024 had dementia - six had advanced dementia108 people chose death by duo-euthanasia (54 pairs) that yearSource: Regional Euthanasia Review Committees (RTE)As well as demonstrating they are suffering unbearably, they must be assessed by doctors as still having the capacity to decide for themselves they want to die. This can cause immense distress in dementia patients thinking about euthanasia, explains Dr Rozemarijn van Bruchem, a geriatrician and ethicist at the Erasmus Medical Centre in Rotterdam."They think… I have that power right now, but now is too soon. But maybe next month is too late. So how do I decide at what point I need to start this process to see if I meet the criteria, to see if I can get euthanasia? And if I wait too long, might I have missed the window?"Dr van Bruchem says it's because euthanasia is legal in the Netherlands that her patients experience this anxiety. And they know permission for an assisted death in cases of advanced dementia is rare. In countries where euthanasia is prohibited, like the UK, people with dementia may face many challenges, but they rarely have to weigh these life-or-death options - as Els did.In 2024, she told the BBC that she and her husband couldn't wait because there was a chance her Alzheimer's would progress. And Jan was committed to dying with Els. He told the BBC that perhaps he was going too soon, but he had lived his life – his life was completed.Jan and Els were very aware of the burden their end-of-life decisions placed on their son. Bas attended all the meetings his parents had with their separate doctors during the euthanasia process. There were open family discussions. Often, we have regrets when a loved-one dies – especially about what may have been left unspoken. This didn't happen to Bas. Two days before Jan and Els' appointment at the hospice on Monday 3 June he wrote them a letter."It was about eight pages," Bas says. "I went to the campervan late in the evening on Saturday night. I read the whole letter to them. It was about our lives, thanking them for what they'd done."Jan and Els were deeply moved. And just as they rarely displayed affection to each other in public, they hadn't usually been demonstrative with their son either."You feel that they love you, but it's shown by doing stuff, not really saying it, or giving you a hug," says Bas. "My mum did [hug] more when she got dementia, but my dad never did – I never got a hug."That changed in the campervan on that last Saturday night. Jan hugged Bas."He did it after that letter.  It was maybe one of the best moments."Everything was said."

schema.headline: Duo-euthanasia: When your parents choose to die

title: 'Please take the job!' - Trump asks UFC boss Dana White to be White House press secretary
description: US President Donald Trump has asked Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White to be White House press secretary, in a social media post."Da
body: US President Donald Trump has asked Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White to be White House press secretary, in a social media post."Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Dana, please take the job!"It was unclear whether the president's public job offer was genuine, although White said later on Saturday: "I'm going to meet with him, we have a meeting on Monday".The vacancy for White House press secretary has been open since mid-October, when Katie Zacharia quit less than five days into the job.Trump's post on Saturday afternoon comes after his fellow Republicans were routed in the US midterm elections, losing their congressional majorities.The president called White "a violent Fighter and Warrior" and asked that he bring a number of high-profile UFC fighters with him on the job "even though some are not from our Country"."We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left," Trump wrote, alongside photos of the six fighters. Following Trump's post, White posted an Instagram photo of himself behind the lectern in the White House press briefing room. "On to the next chapter," White wrote, though it was unclear if the post was tongue-in-cheek. "Hell yeah! Do it, @DanaWhite!" White House communications director Steven Cheung posted on X, as he shared the president's message.White was ringside for a fight in London on Saturday night between British former world champion Chris Billam-Smith and Jamaican-born Briton Cheavon Clarke at the Copper Box Arena.Asked about the Trump offer at a news conference afterwards, the UFC chief executive said he was flying to Washington for a meeting with Trump on Monday. "I got a lot of jobs already," he told reporters."I'm sure we'll have something to talk about after that," he added, without being drawn on whether he was interested in taking on one of the most gruelling jobs in the political arena.CNN cited a source familiar as saying that White had declined the idea.As he noted in the news conference, he already has a number of time-consuming commitments.As well as leading UFC and Power Slap, a regulated slap-fighting promotion league, he has just launched Zuffa Boxing, a professional promotion company.And last year he was unveiled as one of three new board members of Meta, the owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.Famously combative, White has at times clashed with journalists covering the sport during news conferences.He released a clip in 2020 lambasting reporters who had questioned the UFC's decision to hold fights during the pandemic.In 2009, he released an expletive-laden video tirade using an anti-gay slur while rebutting a journalist's story about changes to credential rules backstage at UFC events.White is a longtime ally - and friend - of Trump.When White and his business partners bought the then-struggling UFC organisation for $2m in 2001, the sport's future seemed uncertain.Just five years earlier, Republican Senator John McCain had famously labelled mixed martial arts "human cockfighting", sparking bans in 36 US states."None of the venues wanted [the UFC]," White said in 2025. "They didn't believe in it. They didn't like it, and they were worried about the type of crowd that would show up for this type of event."With mainstream arenas shutting them out, White credits Trump with saving the organisation by hosting two UFC events at the Trump Taj Mahal casino in Atlantic City, New Jersey, in 2001.White became a speaker for Trump's White House campaigns at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.He also appeared on stage for Trump's victory speech in the 2024 presidential election.This summer, the UFC staged a cage match on the White House lawn.

schema.headline: 'Please take the job!' - Trump asks UFC boss Dana White to be White House press secretary

title: Usman Khawaja: I have not thrown anyone under the bus with relevations
description: Usman Khawaja said he has "not thrown anyone under the bus" with revelations about the sandpaper scandal that engulfed the Australia team in 2018.In h
body: Usman Khawaja said he has "not thrown anyone under the bus" with revelations about the sandpaper scandal that engulfed the Australia team in 2018.In his autobiography - Sabr - and in an interview with the Sydney Morning Herald, Khawaja claimed the entire team should take responsibility for the plot to use sandpaper on the ball in the third Test against South Africa eight years ago.At the time, the only players punished were captain Steve Smith, vice-captain David Warner and opener Cameron Bancroft.Speaking in videos posted on Instagram on Sunday to clarify his comments, Khawaja said: "You would have seen when I mentioned it was all of us, that's implying that whether we like it or not, we are all responsible for what happened together."As a team, we need to take that collectively. That is all."But now that everyone's talking, am I going to deny that everyone knew? Nah, I won't deny that, either. But I never speak on behalf of anyone else in my book, contrary to what the headlines in clickbait media would have you think."Other players involved in the Cape Town controversy have repeatedly denied involvement or knowledge of the plot to alter the condition of the ball by rubbing it with sandpaper.Four bowlers who played for Australia in that Test - Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon - remain part of the team. Cummins has been Test captain since 2021.In 2021, the quartet released a joint statement which said they "did not know a foreign substance was taken on to the field".On Saturday, Darren Lehmann, the Australia coach who resigned in the wake of the ball-tampering scandal, also denied Khawaja's claims when he told ABC: "I don't think everyone would have known."Khawaja retired from international cricket in January. He scored 6,229 runs in 88 Tests for Australia.In October, it was revealed that Khawaja had met with Cummins to discuss the contents of the upcoming autobiography.That meeting took place before Australia's recent Test series in South Africa, which the Proteas won 2-1.In the videos on Instagram, 39-year-old Khawaja explained that blame for the plot should have been shared among the entire set-up, not only Smith, Warner and Bancroft."I waited till the [South Africa] series was over. And you know what? I haven't thrown anyone under the bus," Khawaja said."The guys that are currently in the team right now and the other people that were there on the South African tour, including me, we're not the victims."These three guys took the blame for all of us, and they're the victims. Yes, it was tough for everyone, including me. I had sleepless nights, too."Khawaja also defended not revealing his version of the sandpaper saga at the time, or following the bowlers' statement in 2021, and instead waiting for his autobiography."You ask why didn't I say anything in those four years after that while I was still playing? You know what? I never wanted to be the first guy to chat about this," he said."Call me a chicken or whatever you want, I didn't know how to do it because I was still on the team. How was I ever supposed to bring this up when I knew some of my team-mates didn't want to talk about it?"Cricket Australia is yet to indicate a desire to re-open the investigation into the events at Newlands in 2018.A statement from the governing body said: "There has been a great deal of speculation in the eight years since the 2018 Cape Town Test, including extensive media coverage throughout last month's series in South Africa."During this time there has been the ongoing opportunity to present any relevant information, and this remains the case. All relevant information presented to CA to date has been properly considered and we remain comfortable with the findings of our integrity process."

schema.headline: Usman Khawaja: I have not thrown anyone under the bus with relevations

title: Ambika Mod: Ceiling is getting higher for South Asian actors
description: She has previously spoken about not having access to the same "privilege", external some of her fellow actors do when it comes to roles. Fans have que
body: She has previously spoken about not having access to the same "privilege", external some of her fellow actors do when it comes to roles. Fans have questioned why she hasn't gone on to appear in as many roles as her One Day co-star Leo Woodall, who's since appeared in major films including Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy and A24's Anthony Bourdain biopic, Tony.Addressing this remark, Mod tells Newsbeat she thinks "there's definitely an issue in this industry with systemic racism"."I think it is really hard for South Asian actors to really push through. "I feel like the glass ceiling is always getting higher and higher and higher."A report from the Creative Diversity Network, external suggested that representation of minority ethnic groups on and off-screen dropped slightly last year, after a few years of improvement.And similar research from media watchdog Ofcom , externalfound people from certain backgrounds are less well-represented across the UK broadcasting industry.It said "people from minority ethnic groups (across the industry as a whole) only account for 11% of those in senior management roles".It also found under-representation in creative, production and on-screen roles.Mod says she doesn't know if on-screen representation is changing, but says she "won't engage" with a role if she thinks its tokenistic or stereotypical."I've been very, very lucky in my career so far from very early on to play really complex, meaty roles and to have changed the narrative in many ways," she says."And I'm not looking to regress."And when it comes to considering what to take on next, she says she tries to follow advice Dame Emma Thompson once gave her: "There's no such thing as a career, there's only what you do next.""I'm always just trying to focus on what the new challenging thing is going to be, or cool people that I want to work with," she says."And also what's going to be fun, as well."Her latest role as Laila, a lawless agent of the covert Black Doves, attracted her as it subverted a lot of espionage genre tropes.The character is introduced in season two to assist Keira Knightley's agent Helen on a mission as the stakes get even higher for those working with the secretive organisation. Mod says it was "such a good time" working alongside Knightley and getting to do some extreme stunt sequences together. "Honestly, the main reason I wanted to do it was because of all the stunts," she says."Really badass but it was so much fun. "It was just so fun to take down an absolutely staggering number of men in every single episode." The thriller also has a dark humour to it, which aligns well with Mod who often brings a dry wit to her characters.Her comedic career goes back to when she was about 18, and while studying at Durham University she was part of its sketch comedy group.Despite having not done stand-up for about five years, she says she would "love" to do more comedy in the future."I do sometimes think about going back to it," she reveals."I have a lot of stories to tell."

schema.headline: Ambika Mod: Ceiling is getting higher for South Asian actors

title: Swansea mum tries to raise £2.95m for son's dementia treatment
description: The mum of a five-year-old boy with a rare form of dementia has to pay almost £3m for his life saving treatment.Tate McDaid, from Swansea, was diagnos
body: The mum of a five-year-old boy with a rare form of dementia has to pay almost £3m for his life saving treatment.Tate McDaid, from Swansea, was diagnosed with Sanfilippo Syndrome - a form of dementia that just over 100 UK children have - when he was four. In September, the first gene therapy to treat the condition in children was approved in the US.His mum Tammy said she spent "months praying" for its approval but discovered the treatment is to set cost £2.95 million per child, with it unclear how families outside the US can fund this.Health officials from Wales are currently talking to those in the US to see what potential access pathways there are for Tate."I was excited when the treatment initially got approved but then reality hit hard the next day," Tammy said.This was when she read the US price for the one-time treatment, external had been set at $3.95 million.Tammy contacted Ultragenyx, who developed the treatment, in the hope of understanding how families outside the US, who do not have health insurance there, will cover the costs."We understand what they are charging for American citizens, but they've got health insurance," she added."What is it for us in the UK? "Not even just the UK, but everyone else in the world looking for this treatment."Explaining how the US approved drug, FAYUVI, would work for families outside the US, Ultragenyx said: "There is not a single estimate we can provide for the total cost of care for an international patient, as those costs would depend on the patient's individual medical needs and the treating institution."The Society for Mucopolysaccharide Diseases, external, a charity which helps children living with Sanfilippo Syndrome, said about 140 children in the UK have the condition.There is currently no cure for Sanfilippo Syndrome Type A, also called Mucopolysaccharidosis type III (MPS III), but the new drug could delay its onset, and allow Tate to remain active for longer.The condition, described as "childhood Alzheimer's" or "childhood dementia" due to its neurodegenerative nature, causes the gradual loss of abilities, such as walking and eating.It can progress more rapidly after the age of five, which is why Tammy said "it's really a battle of time" for her to raise enough money to get her son the treatment that is not available yet in the UK.She said: "If a millionaire turned around tomorrow and gave us the money, we'd go to the US straight away."With Tate turning six this month, Tammy doesn't believe time is on their side."Tate is already shown signs of cognitive decline," she added."The older he gets the less the treatment will work and the more ability he will lose in the process. "I feel like we are at a turning point and I'm petrified."

schema.headline: Swansea mum tries to raise £2.95m for son's dementia treatment

title: Are you an evening snacker? What you need to know
description: Tempted by snacks before bed? Here's why - and what you can do about itImage source, Getty ImagesByHealth correspondentFigure caption, Love a bedtime
body: Tempted by snacks before bed? Here's why - and what you can do about itImage source, Getty ImagesByHealth correspondentFigure caption, Love a bedtime snack? You're not aloneAppetite peaks in the eveningDespite the fact we spend longer going without food when we are sleeping, research suggests our appetite naturally peaks in the evening, almost regardless of how much we have eaten earlier in the day.Prof James Betts, who researches how the body handles food and energy at the University of Bath, says a big factor is that our "hunger hormone" ghrelin is generally higher later in the day. "While it tends to be suppressed by meals, that really only happens after the first meal of the day, not after lunch or dinner."But what you eat also matters. Meals rich in protein, fibre and volume tend to keep us satisfied for longer.Betts says not having a nutritious or satiating evening meal can lead to a "crash" later, which sees people snack.For others, the fear of waking up hungry during the night is also a motivating factor, while habit plays a role too."If snacking often happens in the same setting, the surrounding cues can start to trigger cravings," says Prof Suzanne Higgs, an expert in appetite at the University of Birmingham."For example, if someone usually snacks while watching TV, simply turning the TV on may make them feel like eating."Why sweet treats are so temptingIt's not just feelings of hunger that increase later in the day. Research suggests our appetite for calorie-dense foods also becomes stronger, driven by the brain's reward system rather than a genuine need for energy."Our liking and wanting for high-fat foods are greater later in the day compared to low-fat foods," says Beaulieu, who splits her time between the University of Leeds and University of Moncton in Canada. "That hedonic drive can override signals of fullness, making us want to snack or eat a dessert even though we're full."Even after a substantial evening meal, foods rich in sugar, fat or salt can continue to activate reward pathways in the brain, helping explain why many people find themselves reaching for something more.So when you find yourself standing in front of the biscuit tin at 9pm, it may not be a lack of willpower. Your biology is stacked against you.Does snacking make it harder to sleep?The evidence is mixed. But certainly eating a large meal late affects digestion and the body's normal preparation for sleep.What about snacking? Here the research becomes less clear.There is some evidence that foods high in refined carbohydrates and added sugars, from white bread and white rice to biscuits and cakes, may be linked to poorer sleep. Researchers think this could be because such foods cause bigger swings in blood sugar levels and may alter some of the hormonal signals involved in regulating sleep and appetite.However, teasing out cause and effect is difficult. People with poor sleep may be more likely to snack on sugary foods."Sleep deprivation is known to not only increase appetite, but also a desire for energy-dense foods," says Prof Jonathan Johnston, a sleep and body clock expert at the University of Surrey. It means it is very difficult to draw firm conclusions on whether snacking in late evening disrupts sleep, says Betts."The evidence is far from clear and perhaps may reflect that some people respond differently to others to different foods before bed."How to snack in a healthier wayFirst, work out what's driving the snacking. If you are genuinely hungry, it may help to make earlier meals more fillingIf snacking is mainly habitual, changing routines and planning snacks in advance can help"Eating while distracted, for instance watching TV, can lead people to consume more because they pay less attention to how much they've eaten," says Higgs.But there's no need to ban evening snacks completely, says Beaulieu. A reasonable portion of something enjoyable is often more sustainableKeep healthy options, such as fruit, yoghurt and nuts availableEven a little chocolate every now and then is not the end of the world"It's OK to eat those craved foods once in a while in moderation."The trick, she says, is to make the healthy choice the default."If those craved foods aren't in the cupboard on a regular basis and a healthy option is, it means you are more likely to choose the healthier option."

schema.headline: Are you an evening snacker? What you need to know

title: Foggy FA Cup tie: How Altrincham v Notts County was described despite poor visibility
description: One of the most important attributes for a commentator is to be able to see the action you are trying to describe but that became a luxury for BBC Spo
body: One of the most important attributes for a commentator is to be able to see the action you are trying to describe but that became a luxury for BBC Sport's Steve Bower when Altrincham hosted Notts County in an FA Cup tie on Saturday.As thick fog enveloped the Moss Lane ground, he could barely see what was going on in a first-round game being televised live on BBC Two."One of the more challenging of my long career, that's about 35 years now," said Bower about the experience."I was reminded by a colleague - maybe I'm a jinx - that we had a similar thing on the BBC about three years ago when we did York against Wigan in the second round and the fog came in."Tonight was worse. From where we were, opposite the dugouts, once the play went to the centre circle and beyond, we couldn't see a thing. "We couldn't see which team had the ball, let alone which player had the ball after about the 60th minute. Bearing in mind it went to extra-time, it was challenging."I just kept looking down at my phone and it was text message after text message from people saying, 'You're sounding great, but I can't see a thing'. In the end, you have to roll with it and do the best you can."National League Altrincham were on for an upset when they took a 2-1 lead against the League One side but a late Callum Roberts equaliser for County took the game to extra-time before the visiting side won on penalties."The frustrating thing is that for an hour it was a really good FA Cup tie, it had everything," said Bower."It was on for another giant-killing script but then the frustrating thing is that it becomes a non-event because, without stating the obvious, people can't see half of it. "Also, it's not then about the tactics, or the shape of it, or the aggression, or the effort because you just can't see it. As a spectacle in trying to describe a game like you normally would, it's impossible."Bower's radio colleagues were not faring much better as they tried to work out what was going on."I can just about see the bright white numbers on their shirts, but I am struggling to see what is happening on the far side of the pitch," said BBC Radio Nottingham commentator Adam Hassell.Former Notts County striker Mark Stallard, who was also speaking on BBC Radio Nottingham, said: "We're looking around, and here in the press box no-one knows where the ball is! It's like a spot-the-ball competition."I played in the Notts County cup side against Wimbledon when it was abandoned - they equalised in the second half and I didn't see any of it!"Stallard later said: "We genuinely cannot see the linesman or the players on the far side. It's slightly farcical having to commentate for radio listeners."The managers of both teams were on the touchline but even they were struggling as tactics went out of the window. "[Notts County boss] Martin Paterson said credit to Altrincham, they were the better team in the first half and, as for the second, I couldn't see it. He was laughing," said Bower. "Neil Gibson, the Altrincham manager, was saying, 'We were trying to get down to pitchside to look tactically at what they had done after those four substitutions. Have they changed shape? Is it a back four? Have they gone to a box midfield? But we just couldn't see'. "So even from a tactical point of view, the players had to stop playing long diagonal passes and things like that because they couldn't see, they were just having to play short five, 10 yard passes so the game changed in that sense as well. "It was very, very close to getting called off."Bower said some of the players told him they couldn't see both goals or the corner flags from the centre circle."It will live long in the memory, that's for sure," said Bower. "Even on the penalties, you were having to rely on the crowd's reaction before committing to the tale. "You couldn't see the goalkeeper's save, for instance, until the first replay came in."The penalties took place in front of Altrincham fans and, while Bower had replays to call on, the Notts County fans "couldn't have seen anything" from the other end as they had to go on "crowd reaction"."Obviously, the Altrincham fans all had their phones on with the lights trying to put the Notts County players off as well in the fog. A unique evening all around."

schema.headline: Foggy FA Cup tie: How Altrincham v Notts County was described despite poor visibility

title: NZ election: Unusually gloomy Kiwis deliver tightest election in years
description: New Zealand voted in a new government as fog choked the capital, Wellington, on Saturday - and the mood was as palpable as the grey weather."It's pret
body: New Zealand voted in a new government as fog choked the capital, Wellington, on Saturday - and the mood was as palpable as the grey weather."It's pretty flat," 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger says. "There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread.""Tired. I think we're all tired," Symone, 28, admits."I didn't even vote," one man in his 40s sheepishly confesses. He couldn't bring himself to tick any of the boxes, he explains, declining to chat further. "Wellington's a bit of a bubble," another voter says, expressing a caveat I heard often, before describing feeling disillusioned.But polling shows this is a pervasive sentiment across the country: the national mood is low and faith in politics is even lower.More than half the country no longer sees it as a land of opportunity, a recent study found, while a similar portion fears that the future looks even worse.Many Kiwis feel the economy is in ruins, there are no jobs, the cost of living has become sky high, the sense of community that used to be a source of national pride is breaking down and there's no sense of genuine progress on policy solutions. A record number of them are abandoning ship in search of brighter futures elsewhere.Saturday's election also saw a record number of voters desert the two major parties, giving neither a clear mandate. But it brought new highs for parties across the spectrum: the left-leaning Greens, the right-wing libertarian Act Party and the centrist Opportunity Party – the latter of which had never won a seat in parliament before but could now hold the balance of power with seven.Many who spoke to the BBC said the country's decline accelerated into a dive during the Covid pandemic. Unemployment is now at an 11-year high and rising. For Kiwis aged under 24, things haven't been this bad in three decades: jobs are so scarce that one in three either cannot get enough work or have none at all.Michael Dawson says he did everything he thought he was supposed to:  finished school, studied a trade and obtained a qualification, and has applied for dozens of jobs. But it's been a year now and the job market is so dire he hasn't had a single interview."It has sucked. A lot... I'm somewhat cynical with the way I think [about the future] now," the 20-year-old says.Zainab Ali, chief executive of support service Youth Inspire, has never seen demand so high, with waitlists for its employment aid workshops stretching into the hundreds.The young people who do make it through their doors on the outskirts of Wellington are disheartened."The things we used to hear from everyone's grumpy uncle around the Christmas table sometimes, our young people are now starting to give us that same feedback: like, 'What's the point?'"Meanwhile, household electricity bills have jumped drastically, partly driven by global supply shocks. New Zealand remains one of the least affordable places on Earth to rent or buy a home. High inflation means every dollar is having to stretch further.The island nation produces enough food to feed its population eight times over, but about a quarter of adults are skipping meals because the price of groceries – set by a supermarket duopoly – is among the highest in the developed world.And the headlines are full of healthcare crises: long waiting lists, chronic understaffing, crumbling health infrastructure and climbing costs for patients. Few stories have captured the state of the system like the death of a man who collapsed in an emergency department toilet after a nine-hour wait in July."There's a segment of the population that are facing real material hardship... and then there's another segment of New Zealanders that are quite anxious that they could be next," political scientist Luke Oldfield, from Victoria University of Wellington, says.Increasingly polarised public debate – around topics like Māori rights and the Treaty of Waitangi, healthcare for LGBT+ people and immigration – have added to the mental load for many in those communities."There's been a few groups feeling like they're being used as a political football," Dr Lara Greaves, who studies Indigenous politics, says.This perfect storm is driving about 180 people to leave the country every day – a record-breaking exodus that is dividing families, shrinking communities and draining talent pools.Siblings Sam and Emily tell the BBC that they love New Zealand but find it hard to keep finding reasons to stay. Their friends are leaving en masse and even their parents have considered moving to Australia."It's not just that you're being rewarded for going to Australia, it's that you're kind of actively being punished for staying here," Sam says.Many of these issues affecting New Zealand are global trends - and it's undeniable that Kiwis' standard of living is better than many others.But these issues are having a corrosive impact on its national identity."It leads to a crisis of confidence about what New Zealand is and where it's going," Helen Clark, who was prime minister from 1999 to 2008, tells the BBC.Her foundation surveys New Zealanders every year about social cohesion, and its most recent report found Kiwis - in particular young people - feel far more isolated than they did a generation ago, attitudes towards multiculturalism are souring and the population is becoming less hopeful.Faith in institutions and leaders has taken an alarming turn: only two out of five New Zealanders trust the government to do the right thing, while less than half of the country trusts the courts."There's a feeling that, really, there's no-one who cares," Clark says.

schema.headline: NZ election: Unusually gloomy Kiwis deliver tightest election in years

title: Turtle to return to sea after 22 years at Irish aquarium
description: Turtle returns to sea after 22 years recovering in Irish aquariumImage source, Oceanworld Aquarium DingleImage caption, Molly the loggerhead turtle ha
body: Turtle returns to sea after 22 years recovering in Irish aquariumImage source, Oceanworld Aquarium DingleImage caption, Molly the loggerhead turtle has been in the care of aquariums since 2004ByAuryn Cox and Holly FleckBBC News NIMary Cronin's children Barry and Aisling were still young when the family found a severely injured sea turtle buried beneath storm debris on an Irish beach.More than 22 years later, Barry and Aisling have grown up and moved abroad and now Molly the loggerhead has left Ireland too.After two decades of gradual rehabilitation and veterinary care advances, the rescued turtle has been released back into the ocean.Because of severe injuries to her front flippers, believed to have been caused by a shark attack, staff feared she might never be strong enough to survive at sea.Molly was rescued by Dingle Oceanworld Aquarium in 2004 and was there until May 2026 when she moved to to Zoomarine Porto d'Abrigo centre in Portugal.She was released about 12 nautical miles off the Algarve coastline on Wednesday 28 October. "We couldn't be any prouder of her. Getting turtles back to the ocean is always our goal, and this is just the start of a new chapter for Molly," Oceanworld Aquarium said in a social media post.Molly is also carrying a satellite tag so the team at Zoomarine can track her. This Facebook post cannot be displayed in your browser. To view this content choose ‘accept and continue’.The BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites. Facebook content may contain adverts.Mary, from Wexford, said she and her children found the turtle while walking on a beach near Castlegregory on the Dingle peninsula in County Kerry after an Atlantic storm."The beach was full of seaweed and debris," she told BBC News  NI."Something moved in the seaweed and there was this turtle."Molly was "cold-stunned" - a form of hypothermia that affects sea turtles in cold waters.The family called the aquarium whose team arrived within half an hour with heated water tanks.Image source, Kevin CroninImage caption, Mary, her son Barry and daughter Aisling discovered Molly the turtle on a beach in 2004Mary named the turtle Molly after her own nickname and the family returned to visit the turtle at the aquarium over the years."As the children got older, it wasn't every year, but we always called in," Mary said."She followed us through life in a very positive way."Now both Barry and Aisling are living in New Zealand, with Barry working as a conservation biologist and Aisling as a teacher - the imprint Molly left on their lives never went away. And because of this Mary said Molly's departure feels familiar."It's kind of like your child getting on an airplane and going across to another continent," she said. "We are thrilled that Molly has returned to her native home and looking forward to reports back on her progress out in the wild."Image source, Zoomarine AlgarveImage caption, Flannery said he believes Molly was about 10 years old when she was rescuedDr Kevin Flannery, the aquariums director and founder, said previous efforts to fit Molly with prosthetic flippers were unsuccessful.During a recent medical check-up, staff discovered she was carrying eggs."It's important that these creatures get back into the wild and they survive and thrive into the future," he told BBC News NI in June, after she left the aquarium.How long can Loggerheads live for?Loggerhead turtles have a long life span and can live from 50 to 80 years - or older. They begin laying eggs between 25 and 35.Flannery said he believes Molly was about 10 years old when she was rescued.She was taken off display for six months and trained to forage and survive independently.The aquarium worked with Zoomarine, which has a specialist turtle rehabilitation centre, to prepare her for the transfer and release into the warm Atlantic waters.Image source, Oceanworld Aquarium DingleImage caption, Molly weighed about 12kg when rescued and now weighs 120kgDNA testing showed Molly is linked to loggerhead turtles from the Gulf of Mexico and it is hoped she can make her way back there.Loggerhead turtles are considered vulnerable, meaning they face a high risk of extinction.Molly may face dangers on her journey back across the open Atlantic including plastic pollution, fishing gear, hooks and boat strikes.Image source, Zoomarine AlgarveImage caption, Zoomarine has a specialist turtle rehabilitation centreFlannery said Ireland would typically see one or two loggerheads washed ashore each year, although five stranded last year alone.He said warming seas linked to climate change could lead to more strandings meaning rescue centres must be prepared.Molly weighed about 12kg (1st 9lb) when rescued and now weighs 120kg (18st 9lb)."We could have her playing full forward for our All-Ireland teams," he said."She's been part and parcel of the aquarium. All the staff got to know her and all the previous staff we've had here down through the 20 odd years. "But these poor creatures are under threat, so it's vital that Molly gets back to breed."

schema.headline: Turtle to return to sea after 22 years at Irish aquarium

title: Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat
description: Figure caption, Fire engulfed Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat in Bavaria last monthByBethany Bellin BavariaPerched on a ridge high up in the
body: Figure caption, Fire engulfed Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat in Bavaria last monthByBethany Bellin BavariaPerched on a ridge high up in the spectacular scenery of the German Alps lie the burned-out ruins of a mountain house called The Eagle's Nest, which is now at the heart of an intense debate about Germany's Nazi past.Known in German as Kehlsteinhaus, the retreat was built by the Nazis in 1938, and frequented by Adolf Hitler and other high-ranking Nazis and their guests. After World War Two it was classified as a historical monument recalling the Nazi era.Last month it was gutted by fire in a suspected arson attack, and some believe it should be completely destroyed, the site returned to nature and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten.But others want it either partially or completely rebuilt, wary of the risk of turning it into a site for Neo-Nazi pilgrimage at a time when Germany is witnessing the resurgence of the far-right.Germany has an "everlasting responsibility to communicate, to deal with our Nazi past", said Isabel Heinemann, professor of contemporary history at Munich's Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität (LMU).But rebuilding the site completely, she warned, would mean putting "highly ideologised or highly ideological architecture" back in place.Image source, Galerie Bilderwelt/Getty ImagesImage caption, Adolf Hitler used the mountain retreat to welcome guestsBefore it was burned down during the evening of 23 October, the Eagle's Nest had been a popular tourist attraction, owned by the state of Bavaria and operating for many years as a restaurant.Visitors would take a bus and then ride the original brass and mirror-panelled lift through the mountain to the Kehlsteinhaus to savour the magnificent views above the town of Berchtesgaden.Once there, they could eat sausages in the beer garden on the Obersalzberg at 1,834m (6,017ft) above sea level, overlooking the Alps.Unlike Hitler's nearby summer residence, the Berghof, which was bombed in World War Two and demolished in 1952, the Eagle's Nest survived the war.Tens of thousands of tourists visited each season, providing an important source of income to the region.In the 1990s, amid concerns that the site did not do enough to confront the crimes of the Nazi past, a museum, the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, was opened close by.Image source, Universal Images Group via Getty ImagesImage caption, Before it was burned down, the Kehlsteinhaus or Eagle's Nest had long been a tourist destination in BavariaAround 15 years ago, a photo exhibit was opened in the Kehlsteinhaus about its history.Although the Eagle's Nest itself was "largely destroyed" by the fire, according to police, the documentation centre survived unscathed.The authorities have not commented on a possible motive, but a 33-year-old man with a history of mental illness has been detained in a secure psychiatric hospital on suspicion of arson.Some feel this is the moment to allow the site to fade into history."It's been torched now. It's been destroyed. I think they should just clear away the rubble and leave the mountain as it should be in its natural state," said Prof Sir Richard J. Evans, a specialist in Nazi Germany at the University of Cambridge.That has happened with "quite a few other Nazi sites", he argued, including the bunker in Berlin where Hitler killed himself: "The bunker was filled in with concrete and a children's playground put on the top of it on the ground."The Kehlsteinhaus was just "a Nazi vanity project" since romanticised by the name Eagle's Nest, he said.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Police say the old Nazi retreat was largely destroyed by last month's fireBut Bavaria's authorities take a different view about the site's future.Both the state's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, and its minister for the arts, Markus Blume, have spoken out in favour of rebuilding the Kehlsteinhaus."We can hardly leave a ruin standing there," Herrmann said.Sven Keller, head of the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, believes it is important not to leave the site in ruins, as that could encourage Neo-Nazi pilgrims, who would be able to hike up there completely undisturbed."We have quite some experience at Obersalzberg with what happens if we clear those sites. Hitler's Berghof was demolished in the 1950s, and in our experience, this does not remove such sites from the mental maps of people," he told the BBC's Today programme.Nor does he believe "a one-on-one reconstruction" of the site is possible, and Blume has made clear on Bavarian radio that "it should not and must not cost the taxpayer anything".Image source, ERIC SCHWAB/AFPImage caption, After Hitler's downfall, US soldiers captured the mountain-top retreat and are seen relaxing here on 4 May 1945Herrmann said they would look for a sensible solution in consultation with historians, given the historically complex circumstances surrounding the building.Heinemann, who also heads the Leibniz Institute for Contemporary History, believes full-scale reconstruction should be "out of the question"."I rather think we can document the state left by the fire and also document the historical remains of the Kehlsteinhaus, and then reconstruct parts in a modern design, to make clear the different layers of time that can be seen in this building," she told the BBC.Germany and Austria have long struggled to deal with the fraught legacy of buildings and sites connected to the Nazi era. With the recent rise of the far-right AfD and the Austrian Freedom Party, the debate over Erinnerungskultur (Culture of Remembrance) has taken on a new urgency.A row broke out recently in Germany when AfD and conservative CDU councillors in a town in Saxony decided to ban "stumbling stones" memorials - embedded small brass plaques in the streets - to victims of the Nazis.In Austria over the summer, a police station was opened in the house where Hitler was born in Braunau am Inn. It followed years of controversy about how the house should be used.The Austrian government said the police presence would help prevent neo-Nazi pilgrims.But others had wanted the house to become a centre of responsibility, actively confronting the Nazi past.As one resident of Braunau am Inn told me, it was a delicate balance between how much to remember and how much to forget.

schema.headline: Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat

title: Labubu sales are slumping. Is the craze over?
description: For years, Labubu dolls seemed unstoppable.Collectors young and old energetically snapped up "blind boxes" - sealed, mystery packages containing the q
body: For years, Labubu dolls seemed unstoppable.Collectors young and old energetically snapped up "blind boxes" - sealed, mystery packages containing the quirky monsters - often paying $15 (£11) or more.Those unable to get the characters they wanted were often prepared to pay much more on the resale market.The hype around the creatures convinced a mega-fan from North Carolina, who goes by the name Ensito, to leave his tech job in 2024 to create Labubu content full-time, travelling as far as Italy and Spain to seek out the latest releases.Ensito has spent more than $50,000 (£37,000) to build his collection of more than 400 Labubus, a figure he tells the BBC he's "embarrassed to say".He even had a row of custom Labubu-like jagged teeth made by a dentist to wear at events.But in recent months, Ensito's once-viral posts about the furry monsters have struggled. "Those videos used to be able to hit 10,000 really quickly but I'm struggling to do that now."Ensito's focus has shifted to other trends like Hello Kitty and squishies.It's a sign that the craze which made parent company Pop Mart worth more than US toy giants Hasbro and Mattel put together may be running out of steam. Analysts believe the Beijing-based brand is struggling to capture excitement beyond a single viral moment.Pop Mart recently reported that global sales in the three months to the end of September had fallen by as much as 50% on the previous year.The drop was particularly steep outside mainland China, with US revenue down by at least 70%.

schema.headline: Labubu sales are slumping. Is the craze over?

title: Ocarina of Time review: Does Nintendo's Zelda remake match its original?
description: But fancy graphics have come at a price - a pivot away from realism into something a bit more cartoonish. Some might even be disappointed by this, giv
body: But fancy graphics have come at a price - a pivot away from realism into something a bit more cartoonish. Some might even be disappointed by this, given the N64 game had quite horrifying elements in places.One was the Skulltula House, a room where people had been morphed into human-spider hybrids."Back when we created the original Ocarina of Time, the means to convey or express ideas was limited compared with what we have now," series producer Eiji Aonuma - who worked on the original game - said."With regard to even the so-called scary elements, we strove to add a touch of the comical."But he told the BBC that enhanced graphics and lighting capabilities unintentionally exaggerated the already-spooky Skulltula House and its potential to strike fear into players."When we carried out the test play, the testers were telling us, 'Oh, this is too scary'," he said. "So of course, in the end product, we've made the necessary adjustments so that we can retain the same balance that we had achieved in the original."At times, the trip down memory lane was captivating. I knew where to go and what to do, thanks to a kind of muscle memory. However, on occasion that took away from the experience - with some tasks achieved too easily and some puzzles too quickly because I recalled their solutions.Some people will love how similar it is, but I have to wonder if Nintendo has played things a bit too safe.I don't think the developers see it that way."Even if the game may look different, we've maintained the essence that the original developers wanted to and hopefully conveyed through the original Ocarina of Time," Fujibayashi said. Don't get me wrong - the game has lots of changes and surprises, and I won't spoil them, but I wish there had been more.Then again, perhaps the best games leave you wanting more.Or as Mike put it: "I loved the original as much as the next person, but I don't think I'll be going back to it."Fans will no doubt wonder whether this is it, or if there will be more Zelda on the horizon. With the franchise's first movie coming next year, there's certainly more to come in the short term.And in the long term, I wondered if with 30 more years of technological advancements, Nintendo might consider remaking the game once again. "I will be long retired," Aonuma said, with a laugh.

schema.headline: Ocarina of Time review: Does Nintendo's Zelda remake match its original?

title: Suffolk town crier crowned one of the world's loudest women
description: Image source, Jaimielee Rendall/BBCImage caption, Brenda Willison holds the records for the loudest female town crier and loudest shout by a womanByJa
body: Image source, Jaimielee Rendall/BBCImage caption, Brenda Willison holds the records for the loudest female town crier and loudest shout by a womanByJaimielee Rendallin Weeting A town crier who has spent nearly four decades turning heads with her voice has earned a place in the Guinness World Records as one of the world's loudest women.Brenda Willison, who lives in Weeting, Norfolk, holds the titles for the loudest female town crier and for having the loudest female shout. Willison, who has been a town crier in Newmarket, Suffolk, since 2013, reached 105.9 decibels while she was battling a cold to win the title, adding: "They wanted me to get over 100 decibels - and I did."Yet she believed there was still room for improvement: "I reached 109 decibels at the British Championships a few years ago, so if somebody beats it, I'll be back!"Figure caption, Willison, who has worked as a town crier across England since 1987, has competed  around the world, including Australia, and in 1993 won the World Town Crier Championship in Niagara Falls, Canada. While her latest Guinness World Record is based on volume, she was keen to point out that town crying was about much more than simply making the most noise.Competitions are judged on clarity, diction, confidence and delivery, as well as loudness."Some people can be very loud, but you can't always understand what they're saying," she said."There is more to it than just shouting."Image source, Jaimielee Rendall/BBCImage caption, Brenda has been a town crier across the country for almost four decadesTown criers have a history stretching back centuries, acting as official messengers long before the arrival of newspapers, radio and the internet.Although the role remains active across the UK, Willison estimates about 10% of town criers in Britain were women and there were even fewer internationally.She said when she took up the role "there were hardly any women doing it".Despite now holding a world record for the power of her voice, Willison said there was no magic formula behind her success.She said she occasionally uses throat pastilles and has tried honey and lemon, but added: "You learn how to use your voice and look after it - mostly, it's practise."Image source, Jaimielee Rendall/BBCImage caption, Brenda has a back garden pub that is aptly named The CrierWillison said it was her family who first spotted her talent, when her daughters submitted an application on her behalf to become a town crier in Peterborough almost 40 years ago. Willison, who at the time was managing cafés at Ferry Meadows Country Park in the city, recalled: "They wrote in and said if mum stood outside one café and shouted 'chips!', people would be able to hear her at the other one - a mile and a half away."The endorsement worked and decades later she has become a two-time world record holder. She said her family was not shocked by her achievements, adding: "My eldest daughter said, 'Well, it doesn't surprise me because you've always been noisy'. "She reckons she can hear me in her house when I'm in the garden."Willison added her husband was also equally unfazed: "He's had to put up with me for 54 years of being noisy!"Do you have a story suggestion for Suffolk? Contact us below.Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: Suffolk town crier crowned one of the world's loudest women
